questions.q: For the reaction \(2\text{N}_2\text{O}_5(g) \rightarrow 4\text{NO}_2(g) + \text{O}_2(g)\), the rate law is found to be \(\text{Rate} = k[\text{N}_2\text{O}_5]\). What is the order of reaction with respect to \(\text{N}_2\text{O}_5\) and the overall order?
questions.a: The order with respect to \(\text{N}_2\text{O}_5\) is 1 (first order) and the overall order is 1. A wrong answer (e.g., saying order is 2 because the stoichiometric coefficient is 2) reveals the misconception that rate law exponents come from the balanced equation rather than experiment.

questions.q: In the reaction \(\text{CHCl}_3 + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow \text{CCl}_4 + \text{HCl}\), the experimental rate law is \(\text{Rate} = k[\text{CHCl}_3][\text{Cl}_2]^{1/2}\). Explain why the exponent for \(\text{Cl}_2\) is \(1/2\) and not 1 (its stoichiometric coefficient).
questions.a: The exponent \(1/2\) indicates a complex reaction mechanism where the rate-determining step involves the dissociation of \(\text{Cl}_2\) into chlorine atoms, so the rate depends on the square root of \(\text{Cl}_2\) concentration. A student who says "it should be 1 because the coefficient is 1" does not understand that rate law is experimentally determined and reflects mechanism, not stoichiometry.

questions.q:
The following initial-rate data were obtained for the reaction \(2\text{A} + \text{B} \rightarrow \text{Products}\) at 300 K:

| Experiment | \([\text{A}]_0\) (mol L⁻¹) | \([\text{B}]_0\) (mol L⁻¹) | Initial Rate (mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹) |
|------------|---------------------------|---------------------------|----------------------------|
| 1          | 0.10                      | 0.10                      | \(2.0 \times 10^{-4}\)     |
| 2          | 0.20                      | 0.10                      | \(8.0 \times 10^{-4}\)     |
| 3          | 0.10                      | 0.20                      | \(4.0 \times 10^{-4}\)     |

Determine the rate law and calculate the rate constant \(k\) with proper units.
questions.a:
Comparing Experiments 1 and 2: \([\text{A}]\) doubles, \([\text{B}]\) constant, rate increases by factor 4 → order w.r.t. A = 2.  
Comparing Experiments 1 and 3: \([\text{B}]\) doubles, \([\text{A}]\) constant, rate doubles → order w.r.t. B = 1.  
Rate law: \(\text{Rate} = k[\text{A}]^2[\text{B}]\).  
Using Experiment 1: \(2.0 \times 10^{-4} = k(0.10)^2(0.10) = k \times 1.0 \times 10^{-3}\) → \(k = 0.20\ \text{L}^2\ \text{mol}^{-2}\ \text{s}^{-1}\).  
A student who gets orders wrong likely misreads the rate ratios; one who forgets units of \(k\) does not grasp dimensional consistency.

questions.q: A reaction \(\text{A} + 2\text{B} \rightarrow \text{C}\) has the rate law \(\text{Rate} = k[\text{A}][\text{B}]^2\). If the volume of the reaction vessel is suddenly halved (doubling all concentrations), by what factor does the initial rate change? Explain.
questions.a: Halving volume doubles \([\text{A}]\) and \([\text{B}]\). New rate = \(k(2[\text{A}])(2[\text{B}])^2 = k \cdot 2[\text{A}] \cdot 4[\text{B}]^2 = 8 \times \text{original rate}\). The rate increases by a factor of 8. A student who says factor 2 or 4 is not applying the orders correctly to the concentration changes.

questions.q: The rate constant for a reaction is reported as \(k = 3.5 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\ \text{L}\ \text{s}^{-1}\). What is the overall order of the reaction? Could this reaction be elementary? Justify.
questions.a: Units of \(k\) for overall order \(n\): \(\text{mol}^{1-n}\ \text{L}^{n-1}\ \text{s}^{-1}\). Given units \(\text{mol}^{-1}\ \text{L}\ \text{s}^{-1}\) match \(n=2\) (second order). The reaction could be elementary if it is bimolecular (e.g., \(\text{A} + \text{B} \rightarrow \text{products}\)) because molecularity = order for elementary steps. A student who says order is 1 or 3 cannot connect units to order; one who says "yes it must be elementary" confuses possibility with certainty — complex reactions can also have integer orders.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using the initial-rates method to determine the rate law for the reaction between sodium thiosulfate (\(\text{Na}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_3\)) and hydrochloric acid (\(\text{HCl}\)) which produces a sulfur precipitate. Outline the steps, what you would measure, and how you would analyze the data.
questions.a: Steps: (1) Prepare several reaction mixtures with varying initial \([\text{Na}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_3]\) while keeping \([\text{HCl}]\) constant, and vice versa. (2) Start each reaction by mixing, and simultaneously start a timer. (3) Measure the time \(t\) for the precipitate to obscure a marked cross beneath the flask (a proxy for a fixed amount of product formed). (4) Initial rate \(\propto 1/t\). (5) Plot \(\log(\text{rate})\) vs \(\log[\text{reactant}]\); slope gives order. A poor answer omits controlling one reactant's concentration or uses only one trial per condition.
